demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: Lin’s life fractures on a Tuesday in November, when her younger brother’s car hydroplanes off a rain-slicked overpass. She sits at her kitchen table, editing a feature on urban housing, when the police knock. By dawn, she stands at a cemetery she has never visited, holding a photo album that suddenly feels like an artifact from a different life. She is thirty-one now, divorced from a marriage that dissolved quietly in the margins of her shock, and working as a staff writer for a regional newspaper. In the weeks that follow, the grief does not arrive as a wave. It settles into the walls. She begins waking at 3 a.m., not to check on an ex-spouse, but because her nervous system has learned to brace for a phone call that never comes. Her sleep grows fractured, stitched together with the sound of tires on wet asphalt and the sharp crack of airbags. During the day, she keeps her press pass and camera bag by the entryway, a habit from her early days as a stringer. She leaves it there because the weight drags her shoulders down, and the metallic clasp sounds like a safety catch. She stops responding to her family’s WeChat group. The messages pile up—photos of her parents’ temple garden, reminders of ancestral tomb-sweeping dates, gentle inquiries about when she will “put the past to rest.” She watches them blur on her screen and turns her phone face-down. At the newspaper, her editor assigns her to cover the anniversary of the city’s transit strike. She sits in the newsroom’s back corner, fingers hovering over her keyboard. Headlines scroll past her screen, but her eyes keep drifting to the parking garage below. She remembers the way the rain pooled in the tire tracks, how her brother’s knuckles had whitened on the steering wheel. She swallows hard, types a single paragraph, deletes it, and starts again. Her byline appears on three consecutive Sundays, but the articles feel thin, like paper stretched too far. She catches herself listening to the hum of the HVAC system, counting the breaths of the colleague sitting next to her, waiting for the floor to drop. Deadlines pass. She submits. She tells herself she is holding it together. When Lin sits in the leather chair across from me now, she arrives precisely eleven minutes early. She always chooses the seat with the clearest view of the door. Her hands rest on her knees, palms up, as if she is bracing to catch something falling. She describes her days as a series of near-misses: a delivery truck backing up too loudly sends her heart into her throat; the smell of wet pavement on the walk to the subway station leaves her standing on the sidewalk until the crowd parts; her ex-husband’s name on a banking portal triggers a cold, heavy stillness that takes an hour to dissolve. She no longer watches news broadcasts about traffic accidents. She tells me she once believed that if she worked fast enough, documented enough, she could outrun the silence that followed her brother’s last text—almost home. Now she knows silence is not empty. It is full of everything that cannot be rewritten.
